question: I don't understand recursion before the DSA CAT. What should I do?
answer: Trace small examples by hand first: draw the call stack for factorial(4) and fibonacci(5) on paper. Then always write the base case before the recursive case. Practise 5 to 6 classic problems (power, reverse a string, sum of digits, binary search) and you will see the same pattern repeat.

question: How do I prepare for the DSA CAT in 3 days?
answer: Day 1: arrays, linked lists and stacks, with one written program each. Day 2: queues, trees and traversals; draw the trees. Day 3: solve past papers under a timer. Write code neatly on paper, because you won't have an IDE in the exam.

question: Linked list pointer questions confuse me. Any tips?
answer: Draw boxes and arrows for every pointer change, step by step, before writing code. Most mistakes are losing the next pointer, so store it in a temp variable first. Practise insert, delete and reverse until you can do them without looking.

question: How should I plan my FFCS registration?
answer: Make two or three backup timetables before registration opens, not one. Check for slot clashes in advance and keep a list of alternate faculty for each course. Log in early and keep your list open next to you so you can switch quickly if a slot fills.

question: How many credits should I take in my first FFCS?
answer: Don't overload in your first semester of choosing. Take a normal load, keep a gap in your timetable for lunch and labs, and avoid stacking all theory classes back to back. Ask your proctor if you are unsure about the minimum and maximum credits for your programme.

question: Do I need to buy a new mini drafter for EG?
answer: No, a used one from a senior works perfectly if the scale and clamp are intact. Check that the scale isn't bent and the screws turn. Keep a sharp pencil set (2H, H, HB) and a good eraser; they matter more than the brand.

question: How do I finish EG sheets faster?
answer: Do the construction lines lightly first and darken only at the end. Practise projections of points and lines until they are automatic, because later topics build on them. Keep your sheets flat in a folder so they don't crease.

question: Which calculus topics should I focus on for CAT?
answer: Focus on the topics your faculty spent the most class time on, and solve every worked example from the class notes again on your own. Past papers from seniors who had the same faculty are the best guide. Practise under a timer, since most marks are lost to speed.

question: Integration problems take me forever. How do I speed up?
answer: Learn to recognise the pattern first: substitution, by parts or partial fractions. Make a one-page sheet with one solved example of each type and revise it daily. Speed comes from doing 10 to 15 problems a day for a week, not from reading.

question: How do I prepare for the physics lab viva?
answer: Know the aim, the formula and why each step is done for every experiment, not just the readings. Most viva questions ask what a quantity means or what happens if you change one thing. Revise your record the night before.

question: How do I keep my chemistry lab record up to date?
answer: Write up each experiment the same day while you remember it. Leave space for observations and get it signed every week. Falling behind is the most common reason people lose record marks.

question: How do I get better at programming as a first year?
answer: Code every day for 30 minutes rather than for 5 hours once a week. Start with simple problems on loops and arrays, then move to functions and strings. When stuck, explain your code line by line out loud; you usually find the bug.

question: How should I prepare for the programming lab exam?
answer: Practise writing full programs without autocomplete, because typing speed and syntax matter. Revise the programs done in lab, and practise reading input carefully. Test with edge cases like zero, negative numbers and empty input.

question: Which clubs should I join in first year?
answer: Join two at most: one technical and one for fun. Go to the first few events of several clubs before deciding, and pick the ones where seniors actually build things or teach. Being active in one club beats being a silent member of six.

question: How do I start doing hackathons?
answer: Start with campus hackathons, where the bar is friendlier. Form a team with mixed skills, pick a problem you personally face, and build a small working demo rather than a big plan. Judges remember a working demo.

question: When should a first year start thinking about internships?
answer: Use first year to build basics: one programming language well, a couple of small projects and a GitHub profile. Serious internship applications usually start from second year. Make a simple one-page resume now and keep updating it.

question: What should go on my first resume?
answer: Education, skills you can actually demo, two or three projects with links, and clubs or hackathons with what you did. Keep it one page. Don't list skills you can't answer questions about in an interview.

question: How do I balance classes, labs and clubs?
answer: Block your timetable gaps for revision and treat them like classes. Keep weekends for club work and assignments. If grades slip before CATs, pause club work for those two weeks; people understand.

question: How do I choose a faculty in FFCS?
answer: Ask two or three seniors who took the same course recently, not just one, because opinions vary a lot. Ask specifically about how they teach and how they grade, not just whether they are 'easy'. Keep a backup faculty for every course in case your first choice fills.

question: Should I take morning or evening slots in FFCS?
answer: Pick the slots that match when you actually focus best, and avoid a timetable with classes from first hour to last hour on the same day. Leave at least one free afternoon in the week for labs, clubs and catching up.

question: What do I do if my FFCS slots clash or a course is full?
answer: Don't panic: switch to your backup timetable, and check whether another faculty offers the same course in a free slot. If something still goes wrong, talk to your proctor early rather than after registration closes.

question: Which courses should I pick in my first FFCS?
answer: Take the core courses your programme requires first, then fill the rest with courses that fit your timetable. Avoid taking too many heavy-lab courses in the same semester. Check the curriculum for your programme so you don't miss a prerequisite.

question: How should I start preparing for CAT exams?
answer: Start about a week before, not the night before. List the units covered, go through class notes first, then solve past papers from seniors who had the same course. Spend the last day only revising, not learning new topics.

question: How is FAT preparation different from CAT?
answer: FAT covers the whole syllabus, so plan unit by unit and start at least two weeks ahead. Re-solve your CAT papers first, since similar questions often come up. Keep a one-page summary per unit for the final revision.

question: Where do I find past papers for exams?
answer: Ask seniors from your branch and clubs; most keep their old papers. Solve them under a timer instead of just reading the answers. Note which topics repeat across papers and prioritise those.

question: I panic during exams and blank out. Any tips?
answer: Do at least one full past paper under real exam timing before the exam, so the format feels familiar. In the exam, start with the question you are most confident about to build momentum. Sleep properly the night before; all-nighters make blanking out worse.

question: How do I start my first project as a first year?
answer: Pick a small problem you face yourself and build the simplest version that works in a weekend. Put it on GitHub with a short README. A small finished project teaches more than a big unfinished one.

question: How do club recruitments work and how do I get selected?
answer: Follow the clubs you like on Instagram so you don't miss recruitment announcements. For technical clubs, show something you have built, even if it is small. Show genuine interest and be honest about what you know.

question: How do I find a team for a hackathon?
answer: Look for people with different skills: someone who codes the backend, someone good with design, someone who can pitch. Classmates and club members are the easiest start. Agree on the problem and roles in the first hour.

question: Can first years do research with professors?
answer: Yes, if you show interest and basic skills. Read a little about a professor's work first, then email or meet them with a specific question. Start small, like helping with data or a literature review.

question: Who do I contact for a hostel problem like water or electricity?
answer: Raise it through the official hostel complaint channel first, and note the date. If it isn't fixed in reasonable time, go to your block warden with the complaint details. Ask your block seniors which channel gets the fastest response.

question: How do I choose a mess type?
answer: Ask seniors in your block about the food quality of each mess type this semester, because it changes. Think about your budget and diet. Check the official rules for when you are allowed to change.

question: I feel homesick and lonely in first year. Is that normal?
answer: Very normal; most people feel it in the first months. Join one club or activity with regular meetings so you see the same people often. Call home on a fixed schedule, and talk to a senior or counsellor if it doesn't ease.

question: What's the best way to get around campus?
answer: Walking is fine for most of the day if your timetable is planned well. Many students buy a used cycle from seniors at the end of the year instead of a new one. Learn the shortcuts between blocks in the first week.

question: What should I buy and not buy as a fresher?
answer: Don't buy everything new: lab coats, scientific calculators, drafters and mattresses are easy to get from seniors at a fraction of the price. Buy only after classes start and you know what your courses actually need.

question: Which coding platform should I start with?
answer: Pick one platform and stick to it for a few months instead of hopping between several. Start with easy problems on arrays and strings, then move up. Consistency matters more than which platform you choose.

question: Should I focus on development or DSA in first year?
answer: Do a bit of both: basic DSA builds problem-solving, and one small development project shows you can build things. In first year, depth in one language and a habit of practising beats chasing everything.

question: Do I need LinkedIn in first year?
answer: A simple profile helps: a clear photo, your programme, and the projects and clubs you are part of. Post when you finish something real. Connect with seniors and alumni from your field.

question: I don't know which direction to choose. How do I decide?
answer: You don't need to decide in first year. Try a few areas through small projects, workshops and club events, and notice what you enjoy doing for hours. Talk to seniors in different fields about what their work actually involves.

question: Physics theory feels abstract. How do I understand it?
answer: Connect each formula to a physical picture: draw the situation before solving. Work through the solved examples in your notes without looking at the answers. Explain a concept out loud to a friend; gaps show up quickly.
